title: Love God, Serve Man -- Ch. 2: A Year of Love and Service
keywords: Outstanding Manilan in Civic Leadership Award
to announce a year of favor
primary_topics: Chapter 2 of 'Love God, Serve Man' -- CJP's June 27, 1991 valedictory as president of the Rotary Club of Manila, reporting how the credo LOVE GOD, SERVE MAN was carried out over his one-year term and insisting that the achievements were not his but the Club's.

An accounting of the year's work in three parts: traditional projects continued, existing programs expanded and improved, and six wholly new projects launched -- the Four-Way Test posters, Ang Katotohanan, the Eye Bank, DISCON '91, the Preserve Planet Earth information blitz, and the Earthquake Relief and Rehabilitation program.

A measured self-assessment against four criteria borrowed from a perceptive analyst -- goals attained, members' participation, financial support and awards received -- yielding about 95 percent of planned projects accomplished, all 72 committees meeting, P22 million raised and spent, and a string of national and international awards.

The closing turn from achievement to love: citing 1 Corinthians 13 and 1 John 4:8, he holds that service, goals and accolades are worth nothing without love, and thanks the Rotarians for their love when he was angry, stubborn, late, proud and wrong.
sub_topics: He opens by recalling that one year earlier he had stood on the same rostrum awed by the responsibilities of leading the oldest and largest civic club in Asia, knowing he was stepping into the shoes of great and honorable men and could steer the Club to nothing less than excellence.

He restates the three-point vision proclaimed at his induction -- members and colleagues, excellence in the professions, business, education and government, and mostly the poor, the afflicted and the weak -- quoting his own inaugural on helping those who cannot help themselves and cannot help us back in return.

He compares the plans to the record: a printed 72-page Program of Action with 178 projects and 67 committees at the start, grown during the year to 185 projects and 72 committees, and now answered by a thicker 94-page Annual Report to be distributed after the address.

First, the traditional projects continued: medico-surgical missions (one held for the first time in Malacanang), the eye clinic and outreach program, health and nutrition education, the anti-drug abuse project, the newsboy Mini-Olympics, the shoeshine stand, essay-writing and oratorical contests, journalism awards, teacher development, employer-employee relations, vocational and career guidance work, the Thursday meetings, the weekly Balita and fellowship activities.

Second, existing programs expanded: the Metro Manila Choral Festival televised for two and a half hours, hands-on computer courses added to the scholarship program, bakery equipment and a mini-bus donated to Sagip Kabataan, the Rotary Village Corps enlarged from 4 to 13 barangays in San Andres Bukid, polio eradicated in 123 Tondo barangays through the immunization of 20,000 babies, a record 14 Paul Harris fellows donating $1,000 each, and a media campaign valued at some P7 million.

Third, the six new projects: 100,000 Four-Way Test posters in English with translations into eight Filipino dialects distributed to barangay centers and sari-sari stores; Ang Katotohanan against lies and distortions in official proceedings, including drafting anti-perjury laws; the Eye Bank with $20,000 from Tokyo South and Kowloon East, a $50,000 RI Foundation grant being finalized and P100,000 from Citibank; DISCON '91, called the most successful ever with a record 2,695 registrants from all 62 clubs in the district; the Preserve Planet Earth blitz estimated to have reached 75 percent of the literate population; and disaster response.

Three disasters in one term: the killer earthquake of July 16, 1990, the most destructive in Philippine history; the devastating typhoon Ruping of September 1990; and the eruption of Mt. Pinatubo in June 1991, whose homeless victims the Club's relief team was attending to even as the valedictory was being held.

Beyond relief to rebuilding: Rotarians not only wrote checks but waded into hands-on service -- medical missions, food, medicine and clothing, a Tent City for 250 families in Burnham Park, contributions to the Red Cross and the Miners' Fund -- then repaired the Juan Luna Elementary School and turned over seven new school buildings in Baguio in time for the school opening.
The four criteria of success he adopts: goals attained, members' participation, financial support, and the accolades and recognition given by the public.

Goals attained: comparing the Program of Action with the Annual Report shows about 95 percent of planned projects accomplished or at least worked on, with unplanned work such as earthquake rehabilitation added as the Rotarians innovated and adapted.

Members' participation: all 72 committees met, some weekly and some occasionally, uniting members across long-established projects, expanded programs and service to the poor, the afflicted and the weak.

Financial support: P22 million in cash and in kind was raised and spent against a previous high of no more than P5 million, with P15 million going to the top three projects -- P8 million for the earthquake fund, P4 million for Preserve Planet Earth and P3 million for DISCON '91.

Awards received: two Best Public Service trophies from the Catholic Mass Media Awards, a Silver Jubilee Community Service Plate from the Legal Management Council, Rotary International trophies, the Outstanding Manilan in Civic Leadership Award from the City of Manila, the Gold Quill from the International Association of Business Communicators, and feature articles in Sunday Panorama and Starweek.
He deflects the personal honors, including the 1991 Best Manilan award, saying he could not have been worthy of them were it not for the Club's monumental achievements in civic work.

The thanksgiving: he thanks the Rotarians for joy, service, comradeship, civic-mindedness and selflessness, but most of all for a love that is inseparably love for God and love for man, extended to him when he was angry, stubborn, late, proud and wrong.

The scriptural close: quoting 1 Corinthians 13 on the noisy gong and clanging cymbal and 1 John 4:8 that God is Love, he calls the year a memorable one of achievement, honors, fulfillment, service and love -- with harried days and near-misses -- an opportunity to announce a year of favor and to give of himself as a Rotarian for others and as a man for God.

notable_anecdotes: The two printed books of the year: a 72-page Program of Action handed out at his induction and a thicker 94-page Annual Report distributed at the valedictory, offered as a record for posterity of what was promised and what was done.
A mission in Malacanang: among the traditional projects continued, he notes that one medico-surgical mission was held for the first time in Malacanang.
Twenty thousand babies: polio was eradicated in 123 barangays in Tondo through an immunization drive, one of the expansions he counts under improved programs.

The earthquake response: on July 16, 1990 the most destructive earthquake in Philippine history struck Central and Northern Luzon, and Rotarians not only wrote checks but put up a Tent City for 250 families in Burnham Park, then repaired the Juan Luna Elementary School and turned over seven new school buildings in Baguio in time for the school opening.
Relief during the valedictory itself: he remarks that even as the Club held its valedictory in the plush Manila Hotel, its relief team was busy attending to the homeless victims of Mt. Pinatubo.

The advertising campaign nobody could miss: he asks who had not heard the Tagalog radio commercials, viewed the television spiel or read the ads, estimating that 75 percent of the literate population saw the Preserve Planet Earth materials.
Thanks for forbearance: he thanks his fellow Rotarians for their love when he was angry, when he was stubborn, when he was late, when he was proud, when he was wrong.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 2 of 'Love God, Serve Man' is CJP's valedictory as president of the Rotary Club of Manila, delivered on June 27, 1991 at the Manila Hotel Fiesta Pavilion, one year after he had stood on the same rostrum awed by the heavy responsibilities placed upon his lean and unworthy shoulders. He restates the three-point vision he had boldly proclaimed under the theme LOVE GOD, SERVE MAN -- members and colleagues, excellence in the professions and government, and mostly the poor, the afflicted and the weak -- and then sets the year's promises against its record: a 72-page Program of Action with 178 projects and 67 committees had grown to 185 projects and 72 committees, and was answered by a 94-page Annual Report distributed that evening. The achievements, he insists, are not his. He accounts for them in three parts: traditional projects continued, from medico-surgical missions to the newsboys' Mini-Olympics; existing programs expanded, including polio immunization for 20,000 babies in Tondo and the enlargement of the Rotary Village Corps from 4 to 13 barangays; and six new projects -- the Four-Way Test posters in eight dialects, Ang Katotohanan, the Eye Bank, DISCON '91 with a record 2,695 registrants, the Preserve Planet Earth media blitz, and the Earthquake Relief and Rehabilitation program born of three disasters, the July 16, 1990 earthquake, typhoon Ruping and the eruption of Mt. Pinatubo whose victims the Club's relief team was attending to even as he spoke. He then measures the year against four criteria: about 95 percent of goals attained, all 72 committees active, P22 million raised and spent against a previous high of P5 million, and awards from the Catholic Mass Media Awards to the Gold Quill, personal honors included that he says he could not have deserved without the Club. He closes by thanking the Rotarians for a love that is inseparably love for God and love for man, quoting St. Paul that without love he would be a noisy gong, and blessing their zeal, faith and love.
